group_assessment.weighting: An NICHD intramural iron-biology laboratory (the Rouault group, which made the original Irp2-null mouse and described the first IREB2 patients) with an NIMH behavioural core. Primary for the gene and its mouse, not for WWOX; they interpret their own model, and the hyperactivity-as-impulsivity reading is speculation they flag as untested.

entries.proposition: Human disease context in the Introduction: biallelic loss-of-function IREB2 (IRP2 absent) with dystonic cerebral palsy, failure to meet milestones, and progressive cerebral atrophy and white-matter loss, frontal predominant (cited human case descriptions).
entries.snippet: The patient was diagnosed with dystonic cerebral palsy and developed a movement disorder. Brain MRIs revealed progressive cerebral atrophy and white matter loss particularly in the frontal regions.

entries.proposition: Mouse severity is stated by the authors to be milder than the human disease.
entries.snippet: The Irp2−/− model significantly differs in severity from the IRP2 patients.

entries.proposition: Motor: rotarod latency to fall reduced by about 40 percent in the null mice; text reports p below 0.05 for the unpaired test; n 26 wild type and 28 null.
entries.snippet: On an accelerating rotarod test Irp2−/− mice had a nearly 40% reduction in latency to fall (Fig. 1A; t = 3.579, df = 40.82, p < 0.05).
entries.anchor: Results, Irp2-null mice show a robust motor deficit

entries.proposition: Body weight confounds the motor readout: null mice were lighter and the genotype effect on hang time was assigned only after weight-covariate ANCOVA.
entries.snippet: This revealed a lower weight in the Irp2−/− mice (Fweight (1,52) = 14.438, p < 0.05; Fig. S2) causing the difference between the groups in their latency to fall during the hangtime test

entries.proposition: The hyperactivity/impulsivity explanation of the motor result is the authors' speculation and is stated as untested.
entries.snippet: the most parsimonious explanation is that the motor deficit in the Irp2−/− mice is related to an increase in maladaptive impulsive behavior and possibly novelty/sensation seeking behavior

entries.proposition: Barnes maze used n = 6 per genotype; the reversal probe target-zone time was 28.97 s in nulls against 22.5 s expected by chance.
entries.snippet: On average, the Irp2−/− mice spent 28.97s (±4.54 SEM) in the target zone which is only slightly above chance (22.5 s).
entries.anchor: Results, Irp2-null mice show poor navigation strategy

entries.proposition: Methods give n = 6 for the Barnes maze cohort.
entries.snippet: Age (5–7 months old) and sex-matched WT and Irp2−/− mice (n = 6) completed the following stages.

entries.proposition: Executive function: touchscreen reversal learning (nine wild type and thirteen nulls, 2-3 months old) showed about threefold more learning errors in nulls.
entries.snippet: Interestingly, there was a greater difference in the number of errors between WT and Irp2−/− mice during the “learning” stage than the “perseverative” stage (28.48 ± 8.7 vs 11.64 ± 5.4 respectively) corresponding with an approximately 3-fold increase in learning errors in Irp2−/− mice.

entries.proposition: The authors say learning, memory and anxiety appear unaffected; the cognitive deficit is reversal-specific.
entries.snippet: Learning and memory and anxiety appear to be unaffected by loss of Irp2, but Irp2−/− mice were consistently hyperactive in novel environments and showed a pronounced reversal learning deficit.

entries.proposition: The authors suggest the mouse phenotype could correspond to humans carrying hypomutations (hypomorphic IREB2 alleles); a suggestion without a human hypomorph measurement.
entries.snippet: The milder disease phenotype of the Irp2−/− mice characterized in this study could be observed in human patients who have hypomorphic mutations of IREB2.

entries.proposition: The authors propose monoamine synthesis (tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylase, iron-dependent) as the vulnerable system, stated as possible and untested.
entries.snippet: Thus, monoaminergic neurons may be particularly sensitive to the functional iron deficiency caused by ablation of Irp2 and may experience a “double hit” of mitochondrial dysfunction and disrupted neurotransmitter synthesis and/or signaling.
